opus-5.5.text:
I think of community design as product design, but the product is the experience of contributing and using the thing, not just the code.

The first principle is that users come first, and you earn their trust by being responsive. In the early days of PyTorch, a lot of us were on the forums and GitHub issues every day, answering questions and fixing bugs fast. When someone files an issue and gets a thoughtful reply within hours, they feel like they're part of something. That's worth more than any feature, and it compounds: those people become your contributors, your evangelists, the ones answering questions for the next wave.

Second, you have to be deliberate about the culture you set, because the early culture tends to stick. If maintainers are dismissive or defensive, that becomes the norm. If they're humble, curious, and willing to say "you're right, we got this wrong," that propagates too. I've always tried to model that we're building this *with* people, not handing it down.

Third, be clear about what the project is and isn't. Open source can drown in feature requests and everyone wanting the project to be a slightly different thing. A clear design philosophy, for us things like being Pythonic, easy to debug, and putting usability before raw performance when we had to choose, gives the community a shared yardstick. It lets you say no gracefully, and it lets contributors make good decisions without asking you.

Fourth, lower the barriers to contribution, but also create real paths to ownership. Good docs, clean contribution guides, labeled starter issues, all of that matters. But the people who stay are the ones who get real responsibility, who become maintainers of a module and get to make calls. You have to be willing to give up control, which is hard, especially for a project you care about.

And finally, governance has to evolve with scale. What works for ten people breaks at a thousand, and breaks again when companies with competing interests depend on you. Being upfront about how decisions get made, and changing that structure before it becomes a crisis, is one of the most important and least glamorous parts of the job.

So mostly it's about empathy, consistency, and caring about people's time. The technology matters, but communities form around how people feel when they show up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shaping community culture and contributor experience through responsiveness, clear principles, and governance, but does not describe designing community-platform software to selectively shape interaction dynamics.

r002.rationale: It notes that early culture tends to stick and that governance must change as a project grows, but does not say Soumith prefers to focus his effort on small-scale community design.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I don't think of it as "designing" a community, because the moment you try to design it top-down, you usually get it wrong. What you can design is the conditions, and then the community shapes itself.

With PyTorch, the thing we cared about most early on was lowering the cost of a first contribution. Not just technically, but emotionally. If someone opens a slightly wrong pull request, or asks a naive question on the forums, how do they get treated? That first interaction decides whether they come back. So we spent a lot of energy on tone: responding fast, being generous, explaining the "why" instead of just saying no. That's not a policy, it's a habit, and habits spread. The early core people set the norm, and newcomers copy what they see.

The second thing is being really clear about who you're building for. In the early days we said, basically, we're building for researchers who want to write Python and have it just work. That clarity is a community design decision, because it tells people what kind of feedback matters and what doesn't. If you try to be for everyone, nobody feels ownership.

Third, I think you have to accept that the community will take the project places you didn't plan. People built things on top of PyTorch that we never anticipated, and some of them became more important than things we did ourselves. Your job at that point is to get out of the way and make the extension points good, rather than pulling everything into the core.

And finally, decision-making needs to be legible. People will tolerate a lot of disagreement if they can see how decisions get made and feel like there's a real path to being heard. What kills communities isn't that the maintainers say no, it's that the no feels arbitrary. So we tried to put design discussions in the open, write down the reasoning, and let people argue with it.

So if I had to compress it: be kind in the small interactions, be clear about who it's for, build good edges so people can extend without permission, and make the process visible. The rest mostly takes care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shaping community conditions, norms, and decision-making, but does not describe community-platform software design as the means of selectively shaping interaction dynamics.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes first contributions and small interactions, saying the early effort focused on tone and on treating newcomers generously.

astra-6.text:
I think community design starts with understanding that open source is about people, not just code. You can put a repository online, but that doesn’t automatically create a community. People need to feel that they can participate and that their participation matters.

So I’d think about the experience of someone showing up for the first time. They ask a question or submit a small patch—what happens next? Does somebody respond? Do you explain why a decision was made? Even if you don’t accept their contribution, can they walk away feeling heard and understanding the reasoning?

There’s also a balance between having a clear technical direction and giving other people room to take ownership. If every decision has to go through the original authors, you’re limiting what the community can become. You want people to develop enough context and trust that they can make decisions themselves.

And a lot of that comes down to consistent behavior. The way maintainers handle disagreement, give credit, and respond to mistakes sets the culture much more than a statement about how welcoming the project is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shaping participation and maintainer behavior, but does not describe community-platform software design as the means for selectively shaping interaction dynamics.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify small-scale community design as Soumith Chintala’s preferred focus for his effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think community design starts with understanding why people would want to participate. They might want to fix something that’s blocking their work, learn how the software works, or build something they’re excited about. You want to make it easy for that first contribution to happen and make sure there’s someone on the other side who listens.

That’s more than having contribution guidelines. How do you respond when somebody proposes an idea you disagree with? Do you explain the constraints? Can they influence the direction of the project, or are they only being asked to implement decisions that have already been made? Those interactions establish the culture.

And as the community grows, you have to give people ownership. If every decision has to go through you, you become the bottleneck. You want people to develop judgment, take responsibility for parts of the project, and eventually help other people participate. To me, that’s a much stronger sign of a healthy community than just counting users or contributions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shaping participation and community culture through project practices, but does not describe community-platform software design as a way to selectively shape interaction dynamics.

r002.rationale: The response discusses giving contributors ownership as a community grows, but does not identify small-scale community design as Soumith Chintala’s preferred focus.
